newsitem.title: USA: American Home to buy rest of Genetics Institute.
newsitem.headline: American Home to buy rest of Genetics Institute.

text.p: American Home Products Corp. said Tuesday it would buy the 40 percent of Genetics Institute Inc. it does not already own for about $1 billion.

The move by Madison, N.J.-based American Home comes less than a week after a Food and Drug Administration advisory panel voted to recommend approval of Genetics Institute's blood clotting therapy, known as BeneFix, for haemophilia B.

American Home Products, the maker of Advil and Anacin pain killers, Robitussin cough remedies and a host of prescription drugs, bought 60 percent of Genetics Institute in 1992 for $666 million. At the time it also received an option to acquire the rest.
Genetics Institute, a Cambridge, Mass.-based biotechnology company, develops drugs through recombinant DNA and other methods.

Under the terms of the 1992 agreement under which American Home acquired its 60 percent interest in Genetics Institute, American Home was granted the option to acquire the remaining interest at prices that escalated to the current exercise price of $85 per share.
Genetics Institute's shares closed Tuesday up $1.75 to $61.75.
Gabriel Schmergel, president and chief executive officer of Genetics Institute, will retire in January 1997, after which he will enter into a consulting arrangement with the American Home.
Patrick Gage, currently chief operating officer of Genetics Institute, will succeed Schmergel as president of Genetics Institute.
American Home said the effect of the acquisition will be to reduce its projected 1997 earnings per share by "less than 3 percent."

American Home said it would take a $700 million writeoff this year for purchased research and development and $300 million will be written off as goodwill. The charges will offset the gain to be reflected in the fourth quarter related to the sale of an 80 percent interest in American Home's food products business.
The company sold the stake in its food business for about $1.3 billion to private investment firm Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst Inc. in September.
